Weber's runs through the sociology of organizations, religion, and the state, through the interpretive and phenomenological traditions, and through comparative-historical sociology. The tension between structure and agency, between social forces that shape individuals and the meaningful action of individuals who make society, which distinguishes Durkheim and Marx from Weber, remains a defining axis of debate, as does the tension between theories of consensus and theories of conflict. The three do not offer a settled body of doctrine to be memorized but a set of enduring questions and a toolkit of concepts for asking them: how societies are held together and pulled apart, how power and inequality are structured and reproduced, how meaning is made and lost, and what the coming of the modern world has done to human life. To read them is to acquire the founding grammar of the discipline and to enter debates that remain unfinished, connecting onward to every later school of social thought.

guides.title: What Sociology Is & How Sociologists Think
guides.summary: An introduction to sociology as a discipline: what it studies, the distinctive way sociologists reason about human life, its founding theories, and the methods it uses to turn observation into evidence.

sections.heading: What Sociology Studies
sections.body: Sociology is the systematic study of human social life, of the groups, institutions, and societies that people create and that in turn shape them. Its subject is not the individual in isolation, which is the province of psychology, but the patterns that emerge when human beings live together: families and friendships, schools and workplaces, religions and governments, cities and nations, and the vast webs of relationship that bind them. The sociologist begins from a deceptively simple observation, that human behavior is powerfully patterned. People do not act at random. Their choices about whom to marry, how to raise children, what work to seek, which god to worship, and how to spend money fall into regularities that vary systematically with their position in society, their class, gender, age, ethnicity, religion, and nation. These regularities can be measured, compared, and explained, and explaining them is sociology's central task. The discipline covers an enormous range of topics. Some sociologists study crime and punishment, others education, health, religion, the media, work, or the family. Some examine large-scale forces such as globalization, industrialization, migration, or the growth of the modern state. Others focus on the fine texture of everyday interaction, how strangers negotiate a crowded sidewalk or how a conversation is managed turn by turn. What unites this diversity is a shared question: how does society, this invisible thing that no one can point to yet everyone lives inside, actually work, and how does it hold together, change, and sometimes fall apart. A useful way to grasp sociology's distinctiveness is to consider a familiar act such as suicide, which seems the most private and individual of decisions. In one of the founding studies of the discipline, Emile Durkheim showed in 1897 that suicide rates are remarkably stable within a society over time and vary predictably between groups, being higher among the unmarried than the married, among Protestants than Catholics, and rising in times of economic upheaval. The individual who takes his own life does so for personal reasons, but the rate at which such deaths occur in a population is a social fact, produced by social forces such as the degree of integration and regulation a person experiences. This is the sociological move in miniature: taking something that appears wholly individual and revealing the social patterning beneath it. Sociology therefore studies not only what is obviously collective, such as governments and markets, but also the social dimension of things that feel entirely personal, our tastes, our emotions, our sense of self. It insists that we are, through and through, social creatures, formed in relationship, and that understanding the human condition requires understanding the society that makes us who we are. That conviction, and the disciplined effort to test it against evidence, is what sociology is.

sections.heading: The Sociological Imagination
sections.body: The heart of how sociologists think was captured by the American sociologist C. Wright Mills in a book called The Sociological Imagination, published in 1959. Mills defined this quality of mind as the capacity to grasp the connection between personal troubles and public issues, between the private lives of individuals and the larger historical and social structures in which those lives are lived. A personal trouble, in his terms, is a difficulty located in the character of an individual and within the range of his immediate relations, something a person experiences as his own private matter and often his own private fault. A public issue transcends the individual, involving the way the many milieus of a society overlap and interpenetrate to form the larger structure of social and historical life. Mills illustrated the distinction with unemployment. When one person in a city is out of work, that is a personal trouble, and to understand it we look at the individual, his skills, his choices, his character. But when fifteen million people are unemployed in a nation of a hundred million, that is a public issue, and no examination of any single individual will explain it. The cause lies in the structure of the economy, the collapse of industries, the movement of capital, forces far larger than any personal failing. The sociological imagination is the trained ability to move back and forth between these levels, to see how the sweep of history and the shape of society press upon the biography of the individual. Its power, Mills wrote, lies in enabling people to understand their own experience and gauge their own fate by locating themselves within their period, to know their own chances in life by becoming aware of those of all individuals in their circumstances. This is more than an academic technique; Mills regarded it as a form of liberation. People often feel trapped by private troubles they cannot name, blaming themselves for hardships that in fact flow from vast impersonal changes such as war, economic depression, or the transformation of family life. To acquire the sociological imagination is to see that many of one's troubles are widely shared and structurally produced, which can transform private anguish into a public matter open to collective action. The sociological imagination also cultivates a distinctive skepticism toward the taken-for-granted. It asks the sociologist to make the familiar strange, to treat customs, beliefs, and arrangements that seem natural and inevitable, the way a family is organized, why some are rich and some poor, what counts as normal, as things that could be otherwise and that vary across time and place. This willingness to question what everyone assumes, and to seek the social forces behind individual experience, is the intellectual signature of the discipline and the single most important habit a student of sociology must acquire.

sections.heading: The Origins of the Discipline
sections.body: Sociology is a relatively young discipline, born in the turmoil of the modern world. Human beings have of course reflected on society since antiquity, in the political philosophy of Plato and Aristotle, the historical writing of the fourteenth-century North African scholar Ibn Khaldun, whose Muqaddimah analyzed the rise and fall of dynasties and the bonds of social solidarity in ways that anticipate later sociology, and the moral and religious teachings of countless traditions. But sociology as a self-conscious discipline, with a name, a method, and an ambition to be a science of society, emerged in Western Europe in the first half of the nineteenth century, and it was a direct response to two great upheavals that shattered the old order. The first was the Industrial Revolution, which from the late eighteenth century transformed how people worked and where they lived. Within a few generations, societies that had been overwhelmingly rural and agricultural, organized around the land, the village, and inherited custom, became urban and industrial, organized around the factory, the city, and the wage. Vast numbers of people were uprooted from the countryside and packed into crowded, often desperate industrial towns. Traditional communities, with their face-to-face bonds and settled expectations, dissolved into the anonymous throng of the modern city. New classes, the industrial working class and the industrial capitalists, confronted one another, and with them came new forms of poverty, exploitation, protest, and disorder. The second upheaval was political. The French Revolution of 1789, following the American Revolution, overturned the ancient assumption that the social order was fixed by God and tradition, that a king ruled by divine right and each person occupied an inherited station. In its place came the revolutionary claims that society is made by human beings and can be remade by them, that authority rests on the will of the people, and that individuals possess rights simply as human beings. These ideas, and the decades of revolution and reaction that followed across Europe, made the nature of society and the sources of social order urgent and open questions. Thinkers confronted a world in which the old certainties had collapsed and asked how any society could hold together at all once tradition and religion had lost their unquestioned authority. It was into this ferment that the founders of sociology stepped. They were driven by a double impulse: a scientific ambition to understand the laws of social life as clearly as physics had grasped the laws of matter, and a practical urgency to diagnose the ills of the new industrial society and find a basis for a stable, just order. Sociology was thus from the start both an intellectual project and a response to crisis, an attempt to make sense of a modern world that had broken decisively with the past and to guide humanity through the disorientation that break had caused.

sections.heading: The Founding Figures
sections.body: Four thinkers are usually credited with establishing sociology, and their ideas still form its foundation. Auguste Comte, a French philosopher writing in the 1830s and 1840s, coined the word sociology itself and gave the discipline its founding ambition. Comte argued that human thought passes through three stages, the theological, in which events are explained by gods and spirits, the metaphysical, in which they are explained by abstract forces, and finally the positive or scientific, in which they are explained by observed laws relating phenomena. He held that society could and should be studied by the same positive scientific method that had triumphed in astronomy and physics, and he envisioned sociology as the queen of the sciences, the last and most complex to mature. Though his grander schemes were soon abandoned, his conviction that society is a proper object of empirical science endured. Karl Marx, the German revolutionary and economist, gave sociology one of its most powerful frameworks even though he never called himself a sociologist. Marx argued that the key to any society is its mode of production, the way it organizes labor to meet material needs, and that history is driven by conflict between social classes defined by their relation to the means of production. Under capitalism, he held, the bourgeoisie who own the factories and the proletariat who sell their labor are locked in an antagonism that shapes everything else and that would eventually issue in revolution. His emphasis on conflict, class, power, and economic structure remains central to sociology. Emile Durkheim, the French scholar who around 1900 secured sociology a place in the university, insisted that society is a reality in its own right, not reducible to the individuals who compose it. He coined the term social fact for the ways of acting, thinking, and feeling that exist outside the individual and exert a constraining force, and he argued that such facts must be explained by other social facts, not by psychology. His studies of the division of labor, of suicide, and of religion demonstrated how rigorous method could reveal the hidden order of social life. Max Weber, the German thinker of extraordinary range, added a crucial complement. Where Durkheim stressed structure and Marx stressed economics, Weber insisted that sociology must also grasp the meanings that people attach to their actions, an approach he called verstehen, or interpretive understanding. He traced the influence of religious ideas on economic life, analyzed the growth of bureaucracy and rationalization, and distinguished class, status, and party as separate dimensions of inequality. Together these four, with the important later recognition of neglected figures, bequeathed the discipline its enduring concerns: order and conflict, structure and meaning, the individual and society, and the distinctive character of the modern world.

sections.heading: The Major Theoretical Perspectives
sections.body: Sociologists do not approach their subject with empty minds. They bring theoretical perspectives, broad frameworks that direct attention to certain features of social life and suggest how those features fit together. Three classic perspectives are usually distinguished, and though the map is a simplification, it remains the standard first orientation. The first is functionalism, descended from Durkheim and elaborated in the mid-twentieth century by American sociologists such as Talcott Parsons and Robert Merton. Functionalism pictures society as a system of interconnected parts, each contributing to the stability and survival of the whole, much as the organs of a body cooperate to keep the organism alive. On this view, institutions such as the family, education, religion, and the economy persist because they perform necessary functions, socializing the young, transmitting values, integrating members, and meeting material needs. Functionalists emphasize shared values, social order, and the way societies tend toward equilibrium. Merton refined the approach by distinguishing manifest functions, the intended and recognized consequences of an institution, from latent functions, its unintended and often unnoticed effects, and by acknowledging dysfunctions, consequences that disrupt rather than sustain the system. The second perspective is conflict theory, descended from Marx and developed by many later thinkers. Where functionalism sees cooperation and consensus, conflict theory sees competition and domination. Society, in this view, is an arena of struggle among groups with unequal power and opposed interests, and social arrangements that functionalists interpret as serving the common good are reinterpreted as serving the powerful at the expense of the weak. Conflict theorists ask who benefits from a given arrangement, how the advantaged maintain their advantage, and how inequality is reproduced and justified. The tradition has expanded far beyond class to analyze inequalities of race, gender, and other dimensions, and it treats change, driven by conflict, as fundamental rather than exceptional. The third perspective is symbolic interactionism, rooted in the work of the American thinkers George Herbert Mead and Herbert Blumer. It operates at a smaller scale than the other two, focusing not on whole societies but on the everyday interactions through which people create and negotiate meaning. Its central insight is that human beings act toward things on the basis of the meanings those things have for them, that such meanings arise in social interaction, and that they are modified through interpretation. Interactionists study how we construct our sense of self through the responses of others, how we present ourselves in daily life, and how shared symbols, above all language, make cooperation possible. These three perspectives are best seen not as rival claimants to a single truth but as complementary lenses. Functionalism illuminates order and integration, conflict theory illuminates inequality and change, and interactionism illuminates meaning and the texture of everyday life. A skilled sociologist moves among them, choosing the lens that best fits the question at hand.

sections.heading: Levels of Analysis: Micro, Meso, and Macro
sections.body: Sociology examines social life at several different scales, and understanding these levels of analysis clarifies both what a study is about and which theories and methods suit it. At one extreme is the micro level, the study of face-to-face interaction among individuals and small groups. Here the sociologist attends to the fine grain of social life: how two people greet each other, how a doctor and patient negotiate a consultation, how a family divides its labor, how a small work team develops its own norms. Micro-level research asks how meaning is created and sustained in the immediate encounters that make up the fabric of daily existence, and it is the natural home of symbolic interactionism and of the closely related traditions of ethnomethodology and conversation analysis, which dissect the taken-for-granted procedures by which people accomplish ordinary social order. At the opposite extreme is the macro level, the study of large-scale structures and processes that operate across whole societies or even across the globe. Macro-level research examines institutions such as the economy, the state, the education system, and organized religion; social categories such as class, race, and gender that sort entire populations; and vast historical transformations such as industrialization, urbanization, the growth of bureaucracy, and globalization. At this scale the individual almost disappears from view, and the sociologist works with populations, rates, and structural relations. Functionalism and conflict theory are characteristically macro-level frameworks, concerned with how societies cohere or divide. Between these poles lies the meso level, an intermediate scale concerned with organizations, communities, and networks, entities larger than a small group but smaller than a whole society. A hospital, a corporation, a university, a neighborhood, a social movement, or a professional association is a meso-level object, and studying it means understanding how such organizations are structured, how they process people, and how they connect the intimate world of individual experience to the sweeping forces of the macro level. One of the enduring challenges of sociology is to link these levels, to show how the choices and interactions of individuals aggregate into large structures, and how those structures in turn shape the individuals within them. This is sometimes called the micro-macro problem, and much sophisticated sociological theory is an attempt to bridge it. The sociological imagination, discussed earlier, is precisely the ability to see the connection across levels, to grasp how a private trouble at the micro level reflects a public issue at the macro level. No level is more real or more important than the others; each captures a genuine aspect of social life. A full understanding of any social phenomenon, from crime to religion to inequality, usually requires attention to all three, tracing how it appears in intimate encounters, how it is organized in institutions, and how it is patterned across the whole of society.

sections.heading: Core Concepts: Structure, Agency, and Socialization
sections.body: A handful of core concepts recur throughout sociology and form the working vocabulary of the discipline. The most fundamental pairing is structure and agency. Social structure refers to the relatively stable, patterned arrangements that exist beyond any individual and that shape and constrain what people can do: the class system, the division of labor, the family form of a society, its laws, its language, its established roles and institutions. Structure is what makes social life predictable; it is the set of rules and resources, mostly inherited rather than chosen, within which every person must act. Agency refers to the capacity of individuals to act, to make choices, to exercise some independent power over their own lives, and even to change the structures that shape them. The relation between the two is one of the great debates of social theory. Do structures determine behavior, so that we are largely products of forces beyond our control, or do free individuals create and remake the social world through their actions? Most sociologists reject both extremes, holding that structure and agency are intertwined: people act within structures they did not create, yet through their actions they reproduce and sometimes transform those structures. The theorist Anthony Giddens captured this with his notion of the duality of structure, arguing that structure is both the medium and the outcome of action, the ever-present condition and the continually reproduced result of the conduct of everyday life. Closely related is the concept of socialization, the lifelong process by which individuals learn the culture of their society, its language, values, norms, and roles, and so become competent members of it. Through socialization, first in the family and then in schools, peer groups, workplaces, and the media, the external structure of society is, so to speak, installed inside the individual, shaping personality, identity, and the very sense of self. Sociologists distinguish primary socialization in early childhood, which lays the deepest foundations, from secondary socialization throughout later life, and they study how socialization varies by class, gender, and culture, producing people fitted to different positions in society. Two further concepts fill out the vocabulary. A norm is a rule or expectation about how people ought to behave in a given situation, ranging from trivial matters of etiquette to grave moral and legal prohibitions; norms are enforced by sanctions, rewards for conformity and punishments for deviation. A role is the set of expected behaviors attached to a particular social position, such as parent, teacher, or police officer, so that a person occupying that position is expected to act in patterned ways regardless of individual personality. Together, structure and agency, socialization, norms, and roles explain how societies achieve their remarkable orderliness, producing coordinated behavior among millions of people, while leaving room for the individuality and the occasional rebellion that keep social life dynamic.

sections.heading: Research Methods: Turning Questions into Evidence
sections.body: What separates sociology from mere opinion about society is its commitment to systematic empirical research, the disciplined gathering and analysis of evidence to test ideas against the world. A sociological study typically begins with a research question or a hypothesis, a proposed answer that can be checked. The sociologist must then decide how to gather relevant data, and here a fundamental choice arises between quantitative and qualitative approaches, each with its own logic, strengths, and characteristic tools. Quantitative research seeks to measure social phenomena numerically and to discover statistical patterns across many cases. Its aim is breadth, generalizability, and precision. The classic quantitative instrument is the social survey, in which a standardized questionnaire is administered to a sample of people, and the answers are coded into numbers and analyzed statistically. Because it is usually impossible to study an entire population, sociologists study a sample and use it to draw conclusions about the whole, which makes the logic of sampling crucial. A representative sample, ideally a random or probability sample in which every member of the population has a known chance of selection, allows findings to be generalized with calculable confidence, whereas a biased sample can badly mislead. Quantitative sociologists also use official statistics, such as census data and crime records, and increasingly the vast digital traces of online life. Their tools include measures of correlation, which capture the degree to which two variables change together, and sophisticated statistical models that attempt to isolate the effect of one factor while holding others constant. Qualitative research pursues a different goal: depth of understanding rather than breadth of measurement, meaning rather than number. It seeks to grasp the social world as those who live in it experience and interpret it. Its signature method is ethnography or participant observation, in which the researcher immerses himself in a community or setting over a long period, watching, participating, and recording, in the tradition of anthropology, in order to understand a way of life from the inside. Another key tool is the in-depth interview, often loosely structured to let respondents speak in their own terms and reveal how they make sense of their lives, and the analysis of documents, texts, and images. Qualitative work sacrifices statistical generalizability for a richness and subtlety that numbers cannot capture, and it excels at generating new insights and understanding processes and meanings. The two approaches are not enemies. Many sociologists now practice mixed methods, combining the two to gain both breadth and depth, using a survey to establish the scope of a pattern and interviews to understand the experience behind it. The choice of method is never arbitrary; it must fit the question, since some questions call for counting and others for understanding, and part of a sociologist's training is learning which tool suits which problem and how to use each one rigorously and honestly.

sections.heading: Variables, Correlation, and Causation
sections.body: At the technical heart of much sociological reasoning lies the analysis of variables and the difficult problem of establishing cause. A variable is any characteristic that can take different values across cases, such as income, age, level of education, religious affiliation, or crime rate. Sociologists are typically interested in relationships between variables, above all in whether one variable influences another. They distinguish the independent variable, the presumed cause, from the dependent variable, the presumed effect that depends upon it. A researcher might hypothesize, for example, that a person's level of education, the independent variable, affects their income, the dependent variable. To investigate such a claim, the sociologist looks for correlation, a systematic relationship in which changes in one variable are associated with changes in another. A positive correlation means the two rise and fall together, as with education and income; a negative correlation means one rises as the other falls, as with education and, in many societies, the number of children a person has. Correlation is measured with precision, and detecting it is the first step in nearly all quantitative research. But here lies one of the most important and most frequently violated principles in all of social science: correlation does not prove causation. That two variables move together does not establish that one causes the other, and mistaking the one for the other is a fundamental error. There are several reasons a correlation may exist without a causal link. The relationship may run in the opposite direction from the one assumed, a problem called reverse causation. Most dangerously, both variables may be caused by some third factor, producing a spurious correlation in which they are related only because each is tied to a common cause. A classic teaching example notes that across towns the number of churches correlates with the number of bars, but neither causes the other; both simply reflect the size of the population. To move from correlation toward genuine causation, sociologists demand more. They require, first, that the cause precede the effect in time; second, that a plausible correlation actually exist; and third, and hardest, that alternative explanations, especially confounding third variables, be ruled out. In the laboratory sciences this is achieved through the controlled experiment, in which the researcher manipulates the independent variable and randomly assigns subjects to conditions, so that other factors are, on average, balanced out. Sociology can rarely run true experiments on whole societies, both for practical and for ethical reasons, so it relies instead on statistical control, using techniques that attempt to hold other variables constant mathematically, and on careful comparison across groups and over time. Establishing cause in the social world remains genuinely difficult, and honest sociologists are cautious about causal claims, often speaking of factors that are associated with or that predict an outcome rather than baldly asserting that one thing causes another. Understanding this care, and the reasons for it, is essential to reading sociological research intelligently and to resisting the constant temptation to leap from a striking correlation to an unwarranted conclusion.

sections.heading: Objectivity, Values, and Ethics
sections.body: Because sociologists study the society they themselves inhabit, and often study matters of deep moral and political concern such as poverty, crime, racism, and inequality, the question of objectivity presses on the discipline with special force. Can the study of society be genuinely scientific and value-free, or does the sociologist's own social position, beliefs, and interests inevitably color the inquiry? Max Weber gave the classic answer over a century ago and it still guides most practitioners. Weber insisted on a distinction between value relevance and value freedom. Our values, he acknowledged, legitimately shape which questions we choose to study; a sociologist troubled by inequality will naturally investigate inequality. But once a question is chosen, Weber argued, the sociologist has a duty to pursue the answer as objectively as possible, following the evidence wherever it leads even when it contradicts his own hopes, and refraining from letting the research double as political preaching. Weber drew a sharp line between statements of fact, about how the social world is, which science can establish, and statements of value, about how it ought to be, which science cannot decide and which the sociologist has no special authority to pronounce. This ideal of disciplined objectivity does not require the impossible feat of having no values; it requires honesty, transparency about one's assumptions, rigorous method, and a willingness to be proven wrong. Modern sociologists add the practice of reflexivity, the deliberate examination of how one's own background and standpoint may influence the research, treating this awareness not as a confession of bias but as a tool for greater accuracy. Alongside objectivity stands the equally serious matter of research ethics, the moral obligations a sociologist owes to the people being studied. Because sociology studies human beings, often in vulnerable circumstances, it can do real harm, and the discipline has developed firm ethical principles enforced by professional associations and institutional review. The first is informed consent: as a rule, people should know they are being studied, understand what participation involves, and agree freely, without coercion or deception. The second is the protection of participants from harm, whether physical, psychological, social, or legal, which means the researcher must weigh risks carefully and safeguard those who take part. The third is confidentiality and privacy: information given by participants must be protected, and their identities concealed in published work, so that taking part does not expose them to embarrassment or danger. These principles arose partly in reaction to notorious past studies that deceived or endangered their subjects, and they sometimes create genuine tension with the pursuit of knowledge, as when full disclosure would change the very behavior under study. Sociologists must navigate such dilemmas thoughtfully, holding that no finding is worth exploiting or harming the people who make the research possible. Objectivity and ethics together express the discipline's dual conscience, its commitment to truth and its responsibility to the human beings who are both its subject and its purpose.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions About Sociology
sections.body: Sociology is frequently misunderstood, and clearing away the common misconceptions sharpens an appreciation of what the discipline really offers. The first and most persistent is that sociology is merely common sense, a matter of stating in complicated language what everyone already knows. In fact a central purpose of sociology is to test common sense against evidence, and it repeatedly finds it wanting. Common sense is a patchwork of folk beliefs, often contradictory, frequently wrong, and shaped by the very society it purports to describe. Sociological research regularly overturns widely held assumptions, showing, for instance, that poverty is caused far more by structural forces than by individual laziness, that criminals are not a distinct type of person set apart from the law-abiding, or that many patterns people attribute to human nature vary dramatically across cultures and epochs. Where common sense offers confident and untested opinions, sociology offers claims disciplined by systematic evidence, and its findings are often surprising precisely because they contradict what everyone assumes. A second misconception is that sociology is the same as socialism, or that it is inherently a left-wing political project. The confusion is understandable given that some founders and many practitioners have held reformist or radical views, and that the discipline studies inequality and power. But sociology is a method of inquiry, not a political program, and its tools are used by scholars across the political spectrum to reach conclusions that sometimes comfort the left and sometimes the right. Conflating the study of society with a particular ideology mistakes the object of analysis for an endorsement of it. A third misconception is that sociology is soft, unscientific, or lacking rigor, mere opinion dressed up with jargon. This underestimates the methodological sophistication surveyed above: careful sampling, statistical analysis, controlled comparison, and rigorous qualitative fieldwork. Sociology is a science in the broad sense of a disciplined, evidence-based, self-correcting search for knowledge, even though its subject, the free and meaning-making human being, makes it harder than the study of atoms and less able to yield exact prediction. A fourth misconception is that sociology denies individual freedom, portraying people as puppets of society. As the discussion of structure and agency showed, mainstream sociology holds a subtler view: individuals act, choose, and create, but always within social conditions they did not make, and recognizing those conditions enlarges rather than denies genuine understanding of human freedom. A fifth is the belief that sociology is impractical, a matter of abstract theorizing with no use in the real world. On the contrary, sociological research informs social policy on crime, health, education, poverty, and discrimination, guides the work of governments, businesses, and charities, and equips citizens to understand the forces shaping their lives. Dispelling these misconceptions reveals sociology as neither obvious nor ideological nor useless, but a distinctive and demanding way of seeing that yields real, tested, and often unexpected knowledge about the social world.

sections.heading: Where Sociology Connects Onward
sections.body: Sociology does not stand alone; it sits within a wider family of social sciences and opens onto a great range of specialized fields, and seeing these connections helps a student place the discipline in the larger map of knowledge. Among its closest neighbors is anthropology, which shares sociology's concern with human social life but has traditionally focused on smaller-scale and non-Western societies and made intensive fieldwork its signature method, though the two disciplines have converged considerably. Psychology is a nearer relative on the individual side, studying the mind and behavior of the person, and the two meet in the hybrid field of social psychology, which examines how individuals think, feel, and act in social settings, how attitudes form, how groups influence their members, and how identity is shaped by others. Economics shares with sociology an interest in markets, work, and the distribution of resources, but tends to model human beings as rational maximizers, whereas economic sociology insists that markets are themselves social institutions, embedded in networks, norms, and power. Political science overlaps with the sociology of the state, power, and social movements. History provides the long view that sociology needs to understand change, and historical sociology deliberately fuses the two, studying how the societies of the present emerged from those of the past. Within sociology itself lies a vast array of subfields, each applying the discipline's imagination and methods to a particular domain of social life. The sociology of the family studies how intimate relationships and household forms are organized and how they vary and change. The sociology of religion, treated more fully elsewhere in this library, examines faith as a social phenomenon. The sociology of education asks how schooling shapes life chances and reproduces or reduces inequality. Criminology studies crime, deviance, and punishment as social products. Medical sociology examines health, illness, and the institutions of care as social as well as biological matters. Urban sociology studies the life of cities; the sociology of work and organizations studies the modern workplace and bureaucracy; and the study of social stratification analyzes the enduring inequalities of class, race, and gender that run through every society. Newer fields address the digital transformation of social life, the environment and society, and the global connections that bind distant places. What holds this sprawling enterprise together is the shared conviction with which this guide began: that human beings are profoundly social, that their lives are patterned by forces larger than themselves, and that those patterns can be understood through disciplined inquiry. A reader who has grasped what sociology studies, the sociological imagination, the founding theories, the levels and core concepts, and the methods and their limits is now equipped to pursue any of these paths, and, more broadly, to look at the ordinary social world, the world of family, work, money, belief, and belonging, with the trained and questioning eye that is sociology's most valuable and most lasting gift.
